opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it really comes down to the fact that health data reflects the population it comes from. Most of the large healthcare AI models we hear about are trained largely on American data, and the U.S. health system is very different from ours. They have different insurance structures, different care pathways, different documentation practices, and different patient populations. So when you take a model built on that data and drop it into a Canadian hospital, you can't assume it will behave the same way. Sometimes it does, but often its performance degrades in ways that are hard to see until something goes wrong.

Canada also has a really distinctive population. We have Indigenous communities with their own health needs and histories, large rural and remote populations, and a lot of linguistic and cultural diversity in our cities. If those groups aren't represented in the training data, the model is going to be less accurate for exactly the people who already face the biggest barriers to care. That's an equity issue, not just a technical one.

Then there's sovereignty and trust. Health data is some of the most sensitive information people have, and Canadians reasonably expect it to be governed by Canadian privacy law and Canadian values. If we rely entirely on models built and hosted elsewhere, we lose a lot of control over how that data is used, how the models are updated, and who benefits from them.

And honestly, I see it as an opportunity. Our single-payer, provincially organized systems mean we have rich, longitudinal data that, done carefully and with the right governance, could support models that are really tailored to how care is delivered here. We have world-class AI research in places like Edmonton, Toronto, and Montreal, and strong clinical research too. Bringing those together lets us build tools that clinicians here will actually trust and use, instead of just being customers of technology designed for someone else's system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts U.S. and Canadian systems in insurance, care pathways, documentation, and populations, but does not say U.S. hospital AI algorithms are optimized for cost savings or that Canada's system is not.

r002.rationale: It gives other reasons for Canadian models, including differences in data, equity, sovereignty, and local care delivery, but does not identify differing cost-saving objectives as a reason.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the simplest way to put it is that a model is only as good as the data it learns from, and most of the big healthcare AI models out there weren't trained on Canadians.

That matters more than people assume. Our population looks different. We have large Indigenous communities, high immigration, rural and remote populations that are hours from a tertiary centre. The way disease presents, the way care is delivered, even the way a clinician writes a note in a Canadian hospital is shaped by our system. We have a single-payer structure, provincial variation, different drug formularies, different imaging protocols. If you take a model built on data from a large American academic centre and drop it into a community hospital in northern Ontario or Saskatchewan, you shouldn't be surprised when it underperforms, and worse, when it underperforms in ways that aren't evenly distributed across patients.

There's also the question of control. Health data is probably the most sensitive data we hold as a country, and I don't think we should be in a position where the models that interpret that data, and the decisions about how they're updated or priced or retired, are made entirely somewhere else. Building our own capacity means we can validate on our own patients, we can be transparent about what went in, and we can hold ourselves accountable through our own regulators and our own institutions.

And frankly, we have the ingredients. Canada has deep AI research talent, places like Amii, Mila and the Vector Institute, and we have longitudinal health records at a population scale that very few countries can match. The gap has been in connecting those two things. So when I say Canada needs its own models, I don't mean we should reinvent everything from scratch. I mean we need models that are trained, evaluated and governed with Canadian patients in mind, so that the benefits actually reach the people here.

r002.rationale: It gives several reasons for Canadian models, including population differences, care delivery, and data control, but does not identify differing cost-saving objectives as one of them.

astra-6.text:
I think Canada needs its own healthcare AI models because those models need to reflect the people we care for and the systems we work in. A model developed elsewhere may learn patterns that don’t translate to Canadian patients or to how care is delivered here. We need to know that it works across our communities, including rural and remote communities, and that it isn’t leaving people behind.

It’s also about having a say in how these tools are built: how patient data is used, what problems we prioritize, and how we measure success. We can collaborate internationally, but we need the capacity here to develop and evaluate models that meet our own healthcare needs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need models that reflect the people we care for and the healthcare system we actually have. A model developed elsewhere may be trained on different populations, different clinical practices, and different ways of collecting data. We can’t assume it will work equally well for patients in Canada.

That doesn’t mean we have to build everything from scratch. But we do need the capacity to develop, adapt, and validate these tools here, with Canadian patients and clinicians involved. And we need to make sure the benefits reach people across the country, including rural and remote communities, while respecting privacy and Indigenous data sovereignty. The goal is better care, and that requires evidence that these models work in our context.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses models reflecting Canadian patients and practices, but does not contrast US hospital algorithms optimized for cost savings with Canada’s system not being optimized for cost savings.

r002.rationale: It does not identify differing US and Canadian optimization objectives as a reason for Canada-specific healthcare AI models.
